claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by extensive motor and non-motor dysfunction, including gait disturbance, which is difficult to treat effectively.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by extensive motor and non-motor dysfunction, including gait disturbance, which is difficult to treat effectively.
evidence: This is a general statement about PD characteristics that draws from established scientific consensus about the disease.

claim: The A13 region is a heterogeneous region of the medial zona incerta (mZI) containing dopaminergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic neurons.
source: This study explores the therapeutic potential of targeting the A13 region, a heterogeneous region of the medial zona incerta (mZI) containing dopaminergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic neurons that has shown relative preservation in PD models.
evidence: This statement describes the cellular composition of the A13 region based on established knowledge about this brain area.

claim: The A13 region has shown relative preservation in PD models.
source: This study explores the therapeutic potential of targeting the A13 region, a heterogeneous region of the medial zona incerta (mZI) containing dopaminergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic neurons that has shown relative preservation in PD models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research showing preservation of the A13 in PD models.

claim: The A13 is identified to project to the mesencephalic locomotor region.
source: The A13 is identified to project to the mesencephalic locomotor region, with a subpopulation of cells displaying activity correlating to movement speed, suggesting its role in locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript (Sharma et al., 2018) showing anatomical projections from A13 to MLR.

claim: A subpopulation of A13 cells displays activity correlating to movement speed.
source: The A13 is identified to project to the mesencephalic locomotor region, with a subpopulation of cells displaying activity correlating to movement speed, suggesting its role in locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research (Li et al., 2021) showing calcium imaging data correlating A13 activity with movement speed.

claim: Photoactivation of the A13 region can alleviate bradykinesia and akinetic features in a mouse model of PD.
source: We show that photoactivation of this A13 region can alleviate bradykinesia and akinetic features, while increasing turning in a mouse model of PD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral improvements with photoactivation.

claim: Photoactivation of the A13 region increases turning in a mouse model of PD.
source: We show that photoactivation of this A13 region can alleviate bradykinesia and akinetic features, while increasing turning in a mouse model of PD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased rotational bias during photoactivation in 6-OHDA mice.

claim: Areas of preservation and plasticity exist within the A13 region in PD models.
source: We identified areas of preservation and plasticity within the A13 region using whole-brain imaging.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data showing preserved TH+ cells and altered connectivity patterns.

claim: There is global remodeling of afferent and efferent projections of the A13 region in PD models.
source: Our findings suggest a global remodeling of afferent and efferent projections of the A13 region, highlighting the zona incerta's role as a crucial hub for the rapid selection of motor function.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data showing changes in connectivity patterns following 6-OHDA lesions.

claim: The zona incerta plays a role as a crucial hub for the rapid selection of motor function.
source: Our findings suggest a global remodeling of afferent and efferent projections of the A13 region, highlighting the zona incerta's role as a crucial hub for the rapid selection of motor function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity data and functional effects observed in the study.

claim: PD is a complex condition affecting many facets of motor and non-motor functions, including visual, olfactory, memory, and executive functions.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a complex condition affecting many facets of motor and non-motor functions, including visual, olfactory, memory, and executive functions (Cenci and Björklund, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on PD symptoms.

claim: Focusing on changes within a single pathway cannot account for all PD symptoms due to the widespread pathology of PD.
source: Due to the widespread pathology of PD, focusing on changes within a single pathway cannot account for all symptoms.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the multisystem nature of PD pathology.

claim: Gait dysfunction is one of the hardest PD symptoms to treat.
source: Gait dysfunction is one of the hardest to treat; pharmacological, deep brain stimulation (DBS), and physical therapies lead to only partial improvements (Nonnekes et al., 2020; Nonnekes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on treatment outcomes for gait dysfunction in PD.

claim: Pharmacological, deep brain stimulation (DBS), and physical therapies lead to only partial improvements in gait dysfunction.
source: Gait dysfunction is one of the hardest to treat; pharmacological, deep brain stimulation (DBS), and physical therapies lead to only partial improvements (Nonnekes et al., 2020; Nonnekes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on treatment outcomes.

claim: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus (GPi) are common DBS targets for PD.
source: While the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus (GPi) are common DBS targets for PD, alternative targets such as pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) and the zona incerta (ZI) have been proposed with mixed results in improving postural and/or gait dysfunction (Caire et al., 2013; Ferraye et al., 2010; Gut and Winn, 2015; Hamani et al., 2011; Moro et al., 2010; Nonnekes et al., 2015; Okun and Foote, 2010; Ossowska, 2020; Stefani et al., 2007; Thevathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on DBS targets.

claim: Alternative DBS targets such as pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) and the zona incerta (ZI) have been proposed with mixed results in improving postural and/or gait dysfunction.
source: While the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus (GPi) are common DBS targets for PD, alternative targets such as pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) and the zona incerta (ZI) have been proposed with mixed results in improving postural and/or gait dysfunction (Caire et al., 2013; Ferraye et al., 2010; Gut and Winn, 2015; Hamani et al., 2011; Moro et al., 2010; Nonnekes et al., 2015; Okun and Foote, 2010; Ossowska, 2020; Stefani et al., 2007; Thevathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on alternative DBS targets.

claim: Most DBS work targeting the ZI has centered on areas close to the STN.
source: Most DBS work targeting the ZI has centered on areas close to the STN (Ossowska, 2020) and recent work shows responses linked to exploratory and goal-directed movements (Hormigo et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ZI DBS targeting.

claim: Recent work shows ZI responses linked to exploratory and goal-directed movements.
source: Most DBS work targeting the ZI has centered on areas close to the STN (Ossowska, 2020) and recent work shows responses linked to exploratory and goal-directed movements (Hormigo et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research on ZI function.

claim: Photoactivation of subpopulations of PPN neurons in PD models shows promise for similar ZI-focused strategies.
source: Recent work with photoactivation of subpopulations of PPN neurons in PD models shows promise for similar ZI-focused strategies (Masini and Kiehn, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on PPN photoactivation.

claim: DBS of the A13 in rat models effectively produces locomotor activity that can be incorporated into ongoing behavior.
source: Indeed, our recent work on preclinical models shows that DBS of the A13 in rat models effectively produces locomotor activity that can be incorporated into ongoing behavior (Bisht et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' own recent work.

claim: The ZI is recognized as an integrative hub, with roles in regulating sensory inflow, arousal, motor function, and conveying motivational states.
source: The ZI is recognized as an integrative hub, with roles in regulating sensory inflow, arousal, motor function, and conveying motivational states (Chometton et al., 2017; Mitrofanis, 2005; Monosov et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on ZI function.

claim: The ZI is well placed to be involved in PD.
source: As such, it is well placed to be involved in PD and has seen increased clinical and preclinical research over the last two decades (Blomstedt et al., 2018; Ossowska, 2020; Plaha et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ZI's functional roles and supported by citations showing increased research interest.

claim: Little attention has been paid to the medial zona incerta (mZI), particularly the A13.
source: However, little attention has been paid to the medial zona incerta (mZI), particularly the A13, the only dopamine-containing region of the rostromedial ZI (Bolton et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and supported by citations.

claim: The A13 is the only dopamine-containing region of the rostromedial ZI.
source: However, little attention has been paid to the medial zona incerta (mZI), particularly the A13, the only dopamine-containing region of the rostromedial ZI (Bolton et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research characterizing the A13 region.

claim: The A13 is preserved in 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-based PD models in primates and mice.
source: Recent research in primates and mice (Peoples et al., 2012; Roostalu et al., 2019; Shaw et al., 2010) indicates that the A13 is preserved in 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-based PD models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on A13 preservation in MPTP models.

claim: It is not clear whether the A13 region substantially remodels in PD animal models.
source: Yet it is not clear whether the A13 region substantially remodels in PD animal models as has been observed for other areas of the brain (Ji et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The A13 located within the ZI projects to two areas of the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), the PPN and the cuneiform nucleus (CUN).
source: Recently, we discovered that the A13 located within the ZI projects to two areas of the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), the PPN and the cuneiform nucleus (CUN) (Sharma et al., 2018), suggesting a role for A13 in locomotor function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior research on A13 projections.

claim: Mini-endoscopic calcium recordings from CaMKIIα populations in the rostral ZI show a subpopulation of cells whose activity correlates with movement speed.
source: Indeed, mini-endoscopic calcium recordings from calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase IIα (CaMKIIα) populations in the rostral ZI, which includes the A13 nucleus, show a subpopulation of cells whose activity correlates with movement speed (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research using calcium imaging.

claim: The A13 region is a potential motor pathway to target for gait improvement.
source: As this region projects to the MLR, it is a potential motor pathway to target for gait improvement, which has been substantiated by our DBS work targeting the A13 in rats (Bisht et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is inferred from anatomical connectivity and supported by citation to DBS work.

claim: Photoactivation of glutamatergic MLR neurons alleviates motor deficits in mouse models that either transiently blocked dopamine transmission or lesioned substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) with 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA).
source: Photoactivation of glutamatergic MLR neurons alleviates motor deficits in mouse models that either transiently blocked dopamine transmission or lesioned substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) with 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) (Fougère et al., 2021; Masini and Kiehn, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on MLR photoactivation.

claim: Kinesia paradoxa in PD patients supports the existence of preserved parallel motor pathways that can be engaged in particular circumstances to produce normal movement.
source: Phenomena such as kinesia paradoxa (Glickstein and Stein, 1991) in PD patients support the existence of preserved parallel motor pathways that can be engaged in particular circumstances to produce normal movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on kinesia paradoxa and inferred from this phenomenon.

claim: Studies show functional changes in A13 following nigrostriatal lesions.
source: Additional support for parallel motor pathways in PD comes from studies showing functional changes in A13 (Hoffman et al., 1997; Périer et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on A13 functional changes.

claim: Nigrostriatal lesions affect cellular function and lead to anatomical remodeling in monoaminergic brain regions including widespread alterations in dopaminergic, noradrenergic, cholinergic, and serotoninergic neuronal populations.
source: Nigrostriatal lesions affect cellular function and lead to anatomical remodeling in monoaminergic brain regions including widespread alterations in dopaminergic, noradrenergic, cholinergic, and serotoninergic neuronal populations; however, global connectivity patterns from A13 have not been explored (Braak et al., 2003; Kish et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2009; Perez-Lloret and Barrantes, 2016; Roostalu et al., 2019; Scatton et al., 1983; Zweig et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on lesion effects.

claim: Global connectivity patterns from A13 have not been explored.
source: Nigrostriatal lesions affect cellular function and lead to anatomical remodeling in monoaminergic brain regions including widespread alterations in dopaminergic, noradrenergic, cholinergic, and serotoninergic neuronal populations; however, global connectivity patterns from A13 have not been explored (Braak et al., 2003; Kish et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2009; Perez-Lloret and Barrantes, 2016; Roostalu et al., 2019; Scatton et al., 1983; Zweig et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The A13 connectome encompasses the cerebral cortex, central nucleus of the amygdala, thalamic paraventricular nucleus, thalamic reuniens, CUN and PPN, superior colliculus (SC), and dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: For example, the A13 connectome encompasses the cerebral cortex (Mitrofanis and Mikuletic, 1999), central nucleus of the amygdala (Eaton et al., 1994), thalamic paraventricular nucleus (Li et al., 2014), thalamic reuniens (Sita et al., 2007; Venkataraman et al., 2021), CUN and PPN (Sharma et al., 2018), superior colliculus (SC) (Bolton et al., 2015), and dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Messanvi et al., 2013; Sita et al., 2007), making the A13 a potential hub for goal-directed locomotion (Choi and McNally, 2017; Eaton et al., 1994; Messanvi et al., 2013; Mok and Mogenson, 1986; Moriya et al., 2020; Ogundele et al., 2017; Sanghera et al., 1991a; Sanghera et al., 1991b; Venkataraman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on A13 connectivity.

claim: The A13 is a potential hub for goal-directed locomotion.
source: For example, the A13 connectome encompasses the cerebral cortex (Mitrofanis and Mikuletic, 1999), central nucleus of the amygdala (Eaton et al., 1994), thalamic paraventricular nucleus (Li et al., 2014), thalamic reuniens (Sita et al., 2007; Venkataraman et al., 2021), CUN and PPN (Sharma et al., 2018), superior colliculus (SC) (Bolton et al., 2015), and dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Messanvi et al., 2013; Sita et al., 2007), making the A13 a potential hub for goal-directed locomotion (Choi and McNally, 2017; Eaton et al., 1994; Messanvi et al., 2013; Mok and Mogenson, 1986; Moriya et al., 2020; Ogundele et al., 2017; Sanghera et al., 1991a; Sanghera et al., 1991b; Venkataraman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity patterns and supported by citations.

claim: Unilateral 6-OHDA injection produced a significant lesion that decreased TH+ neuronal SNc populations.
source: 6-OHDA produced a significant lesion that decreased TH+ neuronal SNc populations. As previously reported (Boix et al., 2015), the SNc ipsilesional to the 6-OHDA injection (n = 10) showed major ablation of the TH+ neurons compared to sham animals (Figure 1C, D: n = 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D comparing TH+ cell counts between 6-OHDA and sham animals.

claim: Unilateral injection of 6-OHDA into the mFB resulted in a significantly greater percentage loss of TH+ cells in the SNc compared to sham animals, regardless of virus type.
source: Unilateral injection of 6-OHDA into the mFB (6-OHDA ChR2: n = 5; 6-OHDA eYFP: n = 5) resulted in a significantly greater percentage loss of TH+ cells in the SNc compared to sham animals (sham ChR2: n = 7 ; sham eYFP: n = 5), regardless of virus type (two-way ANOVA: F1,18 = 104.4, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 6-OHDA lesions produce bradykinetic and akinetic phenotypes in the open field.
source: 6-OHDA lesions produce bradykinetic and akinetic phenotypes in the open field (Li et al., 2022; Magno et al., 2019; Sanders and Jaeger, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on 6-OHDA behavioral phenotypes.

claim: c-Fos expression was found in neurons within the A13 region in photostimulated ChR2 mice.
source: Corroborating the post hoc targeting, we found evidence for c-Fos in neurons within the A13 region in photostimulated ChR2 mice (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: 6-OHDA lesioned animals demonstrated less movement, fewer bouts of locomotion, and less time engaging in locomotion in the open field test.
source: Before post hoc analysis, mice were monitored in the open-field test (OFT), where the effects of the 6-OHDA lesion were apparent, with 6-OHDA lesioned animals demonstrating less movement, fewer bouts of locomotion, and less time engaging in locomotion (Figure 3A–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-I.

claim: 6-OHDA lesioned animals had lower movement speeds than sham control animals.
source: As was expected, 6-OHDA lesioned animals had lower movement speeds than sham control animals (p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of movement speed data.

claim: Photoactivation of the A13 region often generated dramatic effects, with mice showing a distinct increase in locomotor behavior.
source: Notably, photoactivation of the A13 region often generated dramatic effects, with mice showing a distinct increase in locomotor behavior (Figure 3A, Figure 3—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations shown in Figure 3A and videos.

claim: Both sham and 6-OHDA ChR2 mice showed a significant increase in locomotor distance traveled during periods of photoactivation.
source: Both sham and 6-OHDA ChR2 mice showed a significant increase in locomotor distance traveled during periods of photoactivation (Figure 3F, p = 0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of distance traveled data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mice in the ChR2 groups demonstrated an increase in the number of locomotor bouts with photoactivation.
source: Mice in the ChR2 groups demonstrated an increase in the number of locomotor bouts with photoactivation, indicating a greater ability to start locomotion from rest, and that photoactivation was not eliciting a single prolonged bout (Figure 3G, p = 0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of locomotor bout data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Photoactivation increased the total duration of locomotor bouts.
source: Photoactivation also increased the total duration of locomotor bouts (Figure 3I, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of locomotion duration data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The 6-OHDA and sham ChR2 groups displayed increases in average speed in comparison to the 6-OHDA and sham eYFP groups during photoactivation.
source: The 6-OHDA and sham ChR2 groups displayed increases in average speed in comparison to the 6-OHDA and sham eYFP groups during photoactivation (Figure 3H, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of speed data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 6-OHDA ChR2 animals displayed increased ipsilesional rotation with photoactivation.
source: We investigated whether rotational bias persisted during photoactivation and observed that 6-OHDA ChR2 animals displayed increased ipsilesional rotation. Specifically, these animals showed a significant increase in turn angle sum (TAS), indicating enhanced rotational bias with photoactivation toward the lesioned side (Figure 3J, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of turn angle sum data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Sham ChR2 animals showed no significant change in TAS with photoactivation.
source: To determine whether this effect was due to photoactivation alone or its interaction with the lesion, we also analyzed sham ChR2 animals. This group showed no significant change in TAS with photoactivation (Figure 3J, p = 0.06), suggesting that the effect is lesion-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of turn angle sum data in sham animals shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The increased rotational bias in 6-OHDA ChR2 animals is lesion-dependent.
source: To determine whether this effect was due to photoactivation alone or its interaction with the lesion, we also analyzed sham ChR2 animals. This group showed no significant change in TAS with photoactivation (Figure 3J, p = 0.06), suggesting that the effect is lesion-dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between sham and 6-OHDA ChR2 animals.

claim: 6-OHDA mice demonstrated significantly greater times navigating to the base of the pole than sham mice.
source: 6-OHDA mice demonstrated significantly greater times navigating to the base than sham mice (Figure 3L, p = 0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pole test data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Photoactivation of the A13 region led to shorter descent times to the base of the pole in 6-OHDA ChR2 mice compared to 6-OHDA eYFP mice.
source: Photoactivation of the A13 region led to shorter descent times to the base of the pole in 6-OHDA ChR2 mice compared to 6-OHDA eYFP mice (Figure 3L, p = 0.004, Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pole test data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: There was a larger improvement in time to descend from turn with A13 region photoactivation in the 6-OHDA ChR2 mice compared to 6-OHDA eYFP mice.
source: While all groups showed reduced total pole test descent time with photoactivation, considering just the time to descend from turn alone, there was a larger improvement with A13 region photoactivation in the 6-OHDA ChR2 mice compared to 6-OHDA eYFP mice (Figure 3M, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of descent time data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Photoactivation has the effect of reducing bradykinesia by improving the ability of mice to descend the pole during the pole test.
source: These results indicate that photoactivation has the effect of reducing bradykinesia by improving the ability of mice to descend the pole during the pole test.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pole test results showing improved descent times.

claim: TH+ cells in SNc were more vulnerable to the 6-OHDA neurotoxin than those in the A13.
source: As expected (Iancu et al., 2005), our whole-brain imaging results showed that TH+ cells in SNc (Figure 4B, C) were more vulnerable to the 6-OHDA neurotoxin than those in the A13 (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data shown in Figure 4B, C, E, F and a citation to prior research.

claim: 6-OHDA-treated mice showed a significantly greater percentage of TH+ cell loss in SNc compared to the VTA and A13.
source: Specifically, we found that 6-OHDA-treated mice showed a significantly greater percentage of TH+ cell loss in SNc compared to the VTA and A13 (Figure 4G; VTA vs. SNc: p < 0.01; A13 vs. SNc: p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of TH+ cell counts shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Sham animals showed no change in TH+ cell numbers across SNc, VTA, and A13.
source: In contrast, sham animals showed no change in TH+ cell numbers across SNc, VTA, and A13 (Figure 4G, p > 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of TH+ cell counts in sham animals shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The 6-OHDA mouse model effectively replicates the preservation of the A13 region observed in human PD brains.
source: These findings are consistent with observations in the human brain, where the A13 region is preserved in the presence of extensive nigrostriatal degeneration (Matzuk and Saper, 1985). Our results confirm that the 6-OHDA mouse model effectively replicates this aspect of PD pathology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between mouse model data and human observations cited.

claim: Motor-related inputs to the A13 in sham animals exhibited stronger positive correlations across cortical, subcortical, and brainstem regions compared to 6-OHDA mice.
source: Correlation matrix analysis revealed that motor-related inputs to the A13 in sham animals exhibited stronger positive correlations across cortical, subcortical, and brainstem regions compared to 6-OHDA mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In 6-OHDA-lesioned mice, input distribution from dorsal pallidum, lateral hypothalamus, ZI, and tegmental reticular nucleus became positively correlated to somatomotor and somatosensory cortical areas.
source: In 6-OHDA-lesioned mice, input distribution from dorsal pallidum, lateral hypothalamus, ZI, and tegmental reticular nucleus became positively correlated to somatomotor (MOp, MOs) and somatosensory (SSp) cortical areas (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Output patterns from the A13 region showed a higher overall correlation between brain regions in 6-OHDA-lesioned mice.
source: In contrast, output patterns from the A13 region showed a higher overall correlation between brain regions in 6-OHDA-lesioned mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis of efferent patterns.

claim: In sham animals, A13 outputs to cortical regions were negatively correlated with outputs to thalamic, hypothalamic, and midbrain regions.
source: In sham animals, A13 outputs to cortical regions were negatively correlated with outputs to thalamic, hypothalamic, and midbrain regions, indicating a structured and selective projection pattern (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The structured and selective projection pattern observed in sham animals was lost in 6-OHDA mice.
source: This specificity was lost (Figure 5F) in 6-OHDA mice, broader, less targeted distribution of A13 outputs following dopaminergic degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: On the ipsilesional side, there was a decrease in A13 afferent density in 6-OHDA mice compared to sham animals from the primary motor cortex (MOp), primary somatosensory area (SSp), and secondary motor cortex (MOs).
source: On the ipsilesional side, we observed a decrease in A13 afferent density in 6-OHDA mice compared to sham animals from several key regions (Figure 6A), including the primary motor cortex (MOp), primary somatosensory area (SSp), and secondary motor cortex (MOs).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ipsilesional compensatory increases in A13 afferents were observed from the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA), substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), superior colliculus (SCm), and PAG.
source: In contrast, ipsilesional compensatory increases in A13 afferents were observed, for example, from the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA), substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), superior colliculus (SCm), and PAG (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The contralesional side showed a more conservative pattern of afferent remodeling, with a modest decrease in A13 afferent density in primary motor cortex (MOp) and primary somatosensory cortex (SSp) of 6-OHDA mice, with a slight increase in the secondary motor cortex (MOs).
source: Interestingly, the contralesional side showed a more conservative pattern of afferent remodeling, with a modest decrease in A13 afferent density in primary motor cortex (MOp) and primary somatosensory cortex (SSp) of 6-OHDA mice, with a slight increase in the secondary motor cortex (MOs) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Several regions, including the hypothalamus, midbrain, and pons, showed bilateral upregulation of A13 afferents.
source: Several regions, including the hypothalamus, midbrain, and pons, showed bilateral upregulation of A13 afferents, suggesting a more global compensatory response to the unilateral lesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data showing bilateral changes.

claim: Contralesional efferent projection patterns showed increases in efferent density in 6-OHDA mice compared to sham in cortical structures (MOp, MOs, and SSp).
source: whereas contralesional efferent projection patterns showed increases in efferent density in 6-OHDA mice compared to sham in cortical structures (MOp, MOs, and SSp).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data showing contralesional changes.

claim: The increase in efferent projections to the contralesional motor cortices could explain the increased ipsilesional turning bias observed during A13 photoactivation in the 6-OHDA group.
source: This increase in efferent projections to the contralesional motor cortices could explain the increased ipsilesional turning bias we observed during A13 photoactivation in the 6-OHDA group (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity data and behavioral observations.

claim: Photoactivation of the A13 region enhances locomotion in both lesioned and sham mice, increasing distance traveled, locomotion time, and speed.
source: Our results show that photoactivation of the A13 region enhances locomotion in both lesioned and sham mice, increasing distance traveled, locomotion time, and speed.
evidence: This claim summarizes the behavioral results from the study.

claim: In 6-OHDA mice, photoactivation rescued the number of locomotor bouts and significantly improved bradykinesia.
source: Particularly in 6-OHDA mice, it rescued the number of locomotor bouts and significantly improved bradykinesia.
evidence: This claim summarizes specific effects observed in 6-OHDA mice.

claim: Remodeling of the A13 connectivity was observed post-nigrostriatal lesions.
source: Additionally, we observed remodeling of the A13 connectivity post-nigrostriatal lesions.
evidence: This claim summarizes the connectivity findings from the study.

claim: The pro-locomotor functions of the ZI extend further rostrally in the mouse.
source: This study provides direct evidence that photoactivation of the A13 region can drive locomotion, suggesting that the pro-locomotor functions of the ZI extend further rostrally in the mouse.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current study's findings in the context of prior ZI research.

claim: Photoactivation of caudal zona incerta (cZI) neurons increases animal movement speed in prey capture and active avoidance.
source: Previous research has shown that photoactivation of caudal zona incerta (cZI) neurons increases animal movement speed in prey capture (Zhao et al., 2019) and active avoidance (Hormigo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on cZI function.

claim: Early research on the cat suggested a role for the ZI in locomotion, particularly in the region adjacent to the STN, but the effectiveness of rostral ZI regions containing the A13 was not reported.
source: Interestingly, early research on the cat suggested a role for the ZI in locomotion, particularly in the region adjacent to the STN, but the effectiveness of rostral ZI regions containing the A13 was not reported (Grossman, 1958).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to early research on ZI and locomotion.

claim: The A13 is involved in forelimb grasping.
source: Recent work shows that the A13 is involved in forelimb grasping (Garau et al., 2023), suggesting other motor control functions, while a positive valence associated with motivated food seeking behavior has also been reported (Ye et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research on A13 function.

claim: A positive valence associated with motivated food seeking behavior has been reported for the A13.
source: Recent work shows that the A13 is involved in forelimb grasping (Garau et al., 2023), suggesting other motor control functions, while a positive valence associated with motivated food seeking behavior has also been reported (Ye et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research on A13 function.

claim: Previous work targeting the mZI region, including somatostatin (SOM+), calretinin (CR+), and vGlut2+ neurons, did not change locomotor distance traveled in the OFT.
source: Previous work targeting the mZI region, including somatostatin (SOM+), calretinin (CR+), and vGlut2+ neurons, did not change locomotor distance traveled in the OFT (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on mZI neuron populations.

claim: Photoactivation of GABAergic mZI pathways, which project to the cuneiform, promotes exploratory activity by inhibiting cuneiform vGlut2 neurons.
source: Other work has found that photoactivation of GABAergic mZI pathways, which project to the cuneiform, promotes exploratory activity by inhibiting cuneiform vGlut2 neurons (Sharma et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research on GABAergic mZI pathways.

claim: Microinjection of GABAA receptor agonists into the ZI significantly reduces locomotor distance and velocity and may induce cataplexy.
source: Microinjection of GABAA receptor agonists into the ZI significantly reduces locomotor distance and velocity and may induce cataplexy (Chen et al., 2023; Wardas et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on GABAA receptor effects in ZI.

claim: Suppressing GABAergic ZI activity with GABAA receptor antagonists can increase locomotion.
source: Alternatively, while suppressing GABAergic ZI activity with GABAA receptor antagonists can increase locomotion (Périer et al., 2002), chemogenetic or optogenetic inhibition in healthy naive mice can induce bradykinesia and akinesia (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on GABAergic ZI manipulation.

claim: Chemogenetic or optogenetic inhibition of GABAergic ZI in healthy naive mice can induce bradykinesia and akinesia.
source: Alternatively, while suppressing GABAergic ZI activity with GABAA receptor antagonists can increase locomotion (Périer et al., 2002), chemogenetic or optogenetic inhibition in healthy naive mice can induce bradykinesia and akinesia (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research on ZI inhibition.

claim: A13 stimulation did not alter coordination during the pole test task.
source: Given that A13 stimulation did not alter coordination during the task, it suggests a complex behavioral role consistent with its upstream location from the brainstem and its extensive afferent and efferent projections.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pole test results showing improved descent without coordination deficits.

claim: Delays of several seconds are typical when stimulating sites upstream of the cuneiform, such as the dlPAG.
source: Such delays are typical when stimulating sites upstream of the cuneiform, such as the dlPAG, which shows delays of several seconds (Tsang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on dlPAG stimulation.

claim: A13 projections are affected at cortical and striatal levels following 6-OHDA.
source: Our work shows that A13 projections are affected at cortical and striatal levels following 6-OHDA, consistent with our observed changes in locomotor function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the connectivity data from the study.

claim: Over 28 days, there was a remarkable change in the afferent and efferent A13 connectome, despite the preservation of TH+ ZI cells.
source: Over 28 days, there was a remarkable change in the afferent and efferent A13 connectome, despite the preservation of TH+ ZI cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the connectivity and cell count data from the study.

claim: The preservation of A13 is expected since A13 lacks DAT expression and is spared from DAT-mediated toxicity of 6-OHDA.
source: The preservation of A13 is expected since A13 lacks DAT expression (Bolton et al., 2015; Negishi et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2018) and is spared from DAT-mediated toxicity of 6-OHDA (Dauer and Przedborski, 2003; Konnova, 2018; Simola et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on A13 characteristics and 6-OHDA toxicity mechanisms.

claim: Similar timeframes for anatomical and functional plasticity affecting neurons and astrocytes following an SNc or mFB 6-OHDA have been previously reported.
source: Similar timeframes for anatomical and functional plasticity affecting neurons and astrocytes following an SNc or mFB 6-OHDA have been previously reported (Bosson et al., 2015; Perović et al., 2005; Requejo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on plasticity timelines.

claim: Human PD brains that show degeneration of the SNc have a preserved A13 region.
source: Human PD brains that show degeneration of the SNc have a preserved A13 region, suggesting that our model, from this perspective, is externally valid (Matzuk and Saper, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on human PD pathology.

claim: A previous brain-wide quantification of TH levels in the MPTP mouse model identified additional complexity in regulating central TH expression compared to conventional histological studies.
source: A previous brain-wide quantification of TH levels in the MPTP mouse model identified additional complexity in regulating central TH expression compared to conventional histological studies (Roostalu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on TH expression in MPTP models.

claim: There was a downstream shift in the distribution pattern of A13 efferents following nigrostriatal degeneration with a reduction in outputs to cortical and striatal subregions.
source: Still, there was a downstream shift in the distribution pattern of A13 efferents following nigrostriatal degeneration with a reduction in outputs to cortical and striatal subregions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the connectivity data from the study.

claim: The preserved A13 efferents could provide compensatory innervation with collateralization mediated contralesionally and, in some subregions, ipsilesionally to increase the availability of extracellular dopamine.
source: One hypothesis arising from our work is that the preserved A13 efferents could provide compensatory innervation with collateralization mediated contralesionally and, in some subregions, ipsilesionally to increase the availability of extracellular dopamine.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: In a unilateral 6-OHDA model, ipsiversive circling behavior is indicative of intact striatal function on the contralesional side.
source: In a unilateral 6-OHDA model, ipsiversive circling behavior is indicative of intact striatal function on the contralesional side (Carey, 1991; Schwarting et al., 1991; Ungerstedt, 1971; Zetterström et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on rotational behavior in 6-OHDA models.

claim: The predictive value of a treatment is determined by contraversive circling mediated by increased dopamine receptor sensitivity on the ipsilesional striatal terminals.
source: Instead, the predictive value of a treatment is determined by contraversive circling mediated by increased dopamine receptor sensitivity on the ipsilesional striatal terminals (Costall et al., 1976; Lane et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on treatment effects in 6-OHDA models.

claim: A13 stimulation enhances ipsiversive circling and may represent a gain of function on the intact side.
source: Our findings show that A13 stimulation enhances ipsiversive circling and may represent a gain of function on the intact side, but this may be simply due to 6-OHDA mice having reduced locomotion overall.
evidence: This claim is based on the rotational bias data and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Bilateral stimulation of A13 could potentially reduce motor asymmetry and alleviate bradykinesia and akinesia.
source: Given the preservation of A13 cells in PD, bilateral stimulation of A13 could potentially reduce motor asymmetry and alleviate bradykinesia and akinesia.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: With the induction of a 6-OHDA lesion, there is a change in the A13 connectome, characterized by a reduction in bidirectional connectivity with ipsilesional cortical regions.
source: With the induction of a 6-OHDA lesion, there is a change in the A13 connectome, characterized by a reduction in bidirectional connectivity with ipsilesional cortical regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the connectivity data from the study.

claim: In rodent models, the motor cortices, including the M1 and M2 regions, can shape rotational asymmetry.
source: In rodent models, the motor cortices, including the M1 and M2 regions, can shape rotational asymmetry (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Magno et al., 2019; Sanders and Jaeger, 2016; Valverde et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on motor cortex function in rodent models.

claim: Activation of M1 glutamatergic neurons increases the rotational bias.
source: Activation of M1 glutamatergic neurons increases the rotational bias (Valverde et al., 2020), while M2 neuronal stimulation promotes contraversive rotations (Magno et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on M1 function.

claim: M2 neuronal stimulation promotes contraversive rotations.
source: Activation of M1 glutamatergic neurons increases the rotational bias (Valverde et al., 2020), while M2 neuronal stimulation promotes contraversive rotations (Magno et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on M2 function.

claim: A13 photoactivation may have resulted in the inhibition of glutamatergic neurons in the contralesional M1.
source: Our data suggest that A13 photoactivation may have resulted in the inhibition of glutamatergic neurons in the contralesional M1.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism based on the observed rotational bias.

claim: An alternative possibility is the activation of the contralesional M2 glutamatergic neurons, which would be expected to induce increased ipsilesional rotations.
source: An alternative possibility is the activation of the contralesional M2 glutamatergic neurons, which would be expected to induce increased ipsilesional rotations (Magno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about an alternative mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: The ZI could generate rotational bias by A13 modulation of cZI glutamatergic neurons via incerto-incertal fibers, which promotes asymmetries by activating the SNr.
source: The ZI could generate rotational bias by A13 modulation of cZI glutamatergic neurons via incerto-incertal fibers (Ossowska, 2020; Power and Mitrofanis, 1999), which promotes asymmetries by activating the SNr (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a potential mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Unilateral photoactivation of the A13 cells in sham mice failed to produce ipsiversive turning behavior.
source: However, this may only contribute minimally given that unilateral photoactivation of the A13 cells in sham mice failed to produce ipsiversive turning behavior, while unilateral photoactivation of cZI glutamatergic neurons in sham animals was sufficient in generating ipsiversive turning behavior (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data from the study and a citation to prior research.

claim: Unilateral photoactivation of cZI glutamatergic neurons in sham animals was sufficient in generating ipsiversive turning behavior.
source: However, this may only contribute minimally given that unilateral photoactivation of the A13 cells in sham mice failed to produce ipsiversive turning behavior, while unilateral photoactivation of cZI glutamatergic neurons in sham animals was sufficient in generating ipsiversive turning behavior (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on cZI function.

claim: There may be modulation of the PPN neurons responsible for turning behavior with A13 photoactivation.
source: Another possibility involves the A13 region projections to the MLR. With the unknown downstream effects of A13 photoactivation, there may be modulation of the PPN neurons responsible for this turning behavior (Masini and Kiehn, 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a potential mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: The thigmotactic behaviors suggest some effects may be mediated through dlPAG and CUN.
source: The thigmotactic behaviors suggest some effects may be mediated through dlPAG and CUN (Tsang et al., 2021), and recent work suggests the CUN as a possible therapeutic target (Fougère et al., 2021; Noga and Whelan, 2022).
evidence: This claim is inferred from behavioral observations and supported by citations.

claim: Recent work suggests the CUN as a possible therapeutic target.
source: The thigmotactic behaviors suggest some effects may be mediated through dlPAG and CUN (Tsang et al., 2021), and recent work suggests the CUN as a possible therapeutic target (Fougère et al., 2021; Noga and Whelan, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research on CUN as a therapeutic target.

claim: PD is a heterogeneous disease with patient-specific severity, symptoms, and progression.
source: Since PD is a heterogeneous disease, our data provide another therapeutic target providing context-dependent relief from symptoms. This is important since PD severity, symptoms, and progression are patient specific.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about PD heterogeneity.

claim: The CaMKIIα promoter virus is beneficial because it is biased toward excitatory cells.
source: The CaMKIIα promoter virus is beneficial because it is biased toward excitatory cells (Haery et al., 2019), narrowing the diversity of the transfected A13 region, and when combined with traditional therapies, such as L-DOPA, it could be a translatable strategy (Watakabe et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on CaMKIIα promoter specificity.

claim: Optogenetic strategies have been used to activate retinal cells in humans, partially restoring visual function.
source: Optogenetic strategies have been used to activate retinal cells in humans, partially restoring visual function and providing optimism that AAV-based viral strategies can be adapted in other human brain regions (Sahel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on optogenetic therapy in humans.

claim: DBS of the A13 in rats produced robust increases in locomotor activity.
source: Our recent work demonstrates that the A13 is a target for DBS, where stimulation in rats, as predicted, produced robust increases in locomotor activity (Bisht et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' recent work on DBS.

claim: When DBS of the STN is deployed for gait dysfunction in PD, a mixture of unilateral and bilateral approaches has been used.
source: Gait dysfunction in PD is particularly difficult to treat, and indeed when DBS of the STN is deployed, a mixture of unilateral and bilateral approaches has been used (Lizarraga et al., 2016), along with stimulation of multiple targets (Stefani et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on DBS approaches.

claim: DBS does not always have the same outcomes as optogenetic stimulation.
source: DBS does not always have the same outcomes as optogenetic stimulation (Neumann et al., 2023), and our DBS shows a blend of anxiolytic and pro-locomotory effects, as predicted by this work and our work activating GABAergic mZI populations (Bisht et al., 2025; Sharma et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research comparing DBS and optogenetics.

claim: Currently, few PD animal models are available that adequately model the progression and the extent of SNc cellular degeneration while meeting the face validity of motor deficits.
source: Currently, few PD animal models are available that adequately model the progression and the extent of SNc cellular degeneration while meeting the face validity of motor deficits (Dauer and Przedborski, 2003; Konnova, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on PD animal models.

claim: The 6-OHDA models fail to capture the age-dependent chronic degeneration observed in PD.
source: While the 6-OHDA models fail to capture the age-dependent chronic degeneration observed in PD, they lead to robust motor deficits with acute degeneration and allow for compensatory changes in connectivity to be examined.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about 6-OHDA model limitations.

claim: The 6-OHDA lesions resemble the unilateral onset and persistent asymmetry of motor dysfunction in PD.
source: Moreover, the 6-OHDA lesions resemble the unilateral onset (Hughes et al., 1992) and persistent asymmetry (Lee et al., 1995) of motor dysfunction in PD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on PD clinical features.

claim: The MPTP mouse model offers the ease of systemic administration and translational value to primate models; however, the motor deficits are variable and lack the asymmetry observed in human patients.
source: Another option could be the MPTP mouse model, which offers the ease of systemic administration and translational value to primate models; however, the motor deficits are variable and lack the asymmetry observed in human patients (Hughes et al., 1992; Jagmag et al., 2015; Lee et al., 1995; Meredith and Rademacher, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on MPTP model characteristics.

claim: The neurotoxin-based mouse models, such as MPTP and 6-OHDA, offer greater SNc cell loss than genetic-based models.
source: Despite these limitations, the neurotoxin-based mouse models, such as MPTP and 6-OHDA, offer greater SNc cell loss than genetic-based models; in the case of the 6-OHDA model, it captures many aspects of motor dysfunctions in PD (Dauer and Przedborski, 2003; Jagmag et al., 2015; Konnova, 2018; Simola et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research comparing PD model types.

claim: In human PD, there is no significant change in A13 TH+ cell counts.
source: As in human PD, we found no significant change in A13 TH+ cell counts (Matzuk and Saper, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data and a citation to prior research on human PD.

claim: Since A13 neurons remained intact following a lesion, it is possible that changes in the connectome reflected secondary effects from other regions impacted by the 6-OHDA lesion.
source: Another limitation is that since A13 neurons remained intact following a lesion, it is possible that changes in the connectome reflected secondary effects from other regions impacted by the 6-OHDA lesion.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding the interpretation of connectivity changes.

claim: The fact that there was a significant change in the connectome post-6-OHDA injection and striatonigral degeneration is in and of itself important to document.
source: However, the fact that there was a significant change in the connectome post-6-OHDA injection and striatonigral degeneration is in and of itself important to document.
evidence: This claim emphasizes the importance of the connectivity findings regardless of mechanism.

claim: The whole-brain anatomical data offer a correlative framework for understanding the neural circuits involved in A13-mediated locomotor control and its modulation in the 6-OHDA model.
source: Finally, it is important to note that our whole-brain anatomical data offer a correlative framework for understanding the neural circuits involved in A13-mediated locomotor control and its modulation in the 6-OHDA model. However, these data do not establish direct causal relationships.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding the correlative nature of the connectivity data.

claim: Future studies employing techniques such as targeted pathway manipulations or lesioning will be essential to definitively prove the functional necessity of specific connections in mediating the observed behavioral effects.
source: Future studies employing techniques such as targeted pathway manipulations (e.g., optogenetics and chemogenetics) or lesioning will be essential to definitively prove the functional necessity of specific connections in mediating the observed behavioral effects.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions needed to establish causality.

claim: A primary limitation of the whole-brain connectomic screen is the small sample size.
source: A primary limitation of our whole-brain connectomic screen is the small sample size. This restricts the statistical power of our comparisons, and the imaging should be viewed as a preliminary, exploratory screen that provides valuable initial insights into the potential reorganization of the A13 connectome in the 6-OHDA model.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding the connectivity study.

claim: The global approach allows identification of widespread changes in connectivity that might be overlooked by more targeted analyses.
source: That said, the global approach allows us to identify widespread changes in connectivity that might be overlooked by more targeted analyses, offering insights into the complex neural adaptations that occur following nigrostriatal degeneration.
evidence: This claim highlights the value of the whole-brain imaging approach despite its limitations.

claim: The A13 region drives locomotor activity and mitigates bradykinetic and akinetic deficits linked to impaired DAergic transmission.
source: Our research underscores the role of the A13 region beyond the classic nigrostriatal axis in PD, driving locomotor activity and mitigating bradykinetic and akinetic deficits linked to impaired DAergic transmission.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: A13 photoactivation produced a rescue of locomotion loss in 6-OHDA-lesioned mice, as well as bradykinesia.
source: This observation indicates a rescue of locomotion loss in 6-OHDA-lesioned mice, as well as bradykinesia.
evidence: This claim summarizes the therapeutic effects observed in the study.

claim: A13 photoactivation produced possible gain-of-function effects, such as circling behavior, which may be attributed to plasticity changes induced by the 6-OHDA lesions.
source: Additionally, it produced possible gain-of-function effects, such as circling behavior, which may be attributed to plasticity changes induced by the 6-OHDA lesions.
evidence: This claim summarizes the additional effects observed and speculates on their origin.

claim: Widespread remodeling of the A13 region connectome is critical to understanding the effects of dopamine loss in PD models.
source: Widespread remodeling of the A13 region connectome is critical to our understanding of the effects of dopamine loss in PD models.
evidence: This claim emphasizes the importance of the connectivity findings.

claim: The findings support an exciting role for the A13 region in locomotion with demonstrated benefits in a mouse PD model.
source: In summary, our findings support an exciting role for the A13 region in locomotion with demonstrated benefits in a mouse PD model and contribute to our understanding of heterogeneity in PD.
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall significance of the study.

claim: 6-OHDA ChR2 animals showed a reliable pro-locomotion phenotype with A13 region photoactivation.
source: 6-OHDA ChR2 animals showed a reliable pro-locomotion phenotype with A13 region photoactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, p = 0.042).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of trial success rates shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no effect of photoactivation on the probability of engaging in locomotion in the control 6-OHDA eYFP group.
source: As was expected in the control 6-OHDA eYFP group, there was no effect of photoactivation on the probability of engaging in locomotion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, p = 0.71).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of trial success rates in control animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no difference in the time to initiate locomotion between the sham and 6-OHDA ChR2 groups.
source: There was no difference in the time to initiate locomotion between the sham and 6-OHDA ChR2 groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, p = 0.95).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of latency data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: When TAS was calculated only during locomotor periods, the rotational bias was no longer significant.
source: Next, we assessed whether the elevated TAS in 6-OHDA ChR2 animals occurred during locomotion. When TAS was calculated only during locomotor periods, the rotational bias was no longer significant (p > 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of turn angle sum during locomotion.

claim: Neither of the eYFP groups showed any changes in the time to complete the pole test.
source: Neither of the eYFP groups showed any changes in the time to complete the pole test (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by pole test data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: There was an increase in c-Fos fluorescence intensity after photoactivation in 6-OHDA ChR2 mice.
source: (F) Graph shows an increase in c-Fos fluorescence intensity after photoactivation in 6-OHDA ChR2 mice (p = 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of c-Fos expression shown in Figure 2F.
